Figure 2. VIRAL teacher-student pipeline. Phase 1: In simulation, a privileged RL teacher policy πteacher receives full-state proprioception
and exteroception of the task information and outputs WBC commands. Phase 2: A vision-based student policy πstudent observes only RGB
images and sim-to-real proprioception and is trained to imitate the teacher policy via DAgger and behavior cloning.

                                                                     4
Student Element #3: Distributed Simulation Learning
System. Large-scale visual simulation is substantially more
expensive than rendering-free physics, typically operating
at least an order of magnitude slower in terms of simulation
throughput. To scale up visual simulation training through-
put, we implement a customized version of TRL [68] with
support of Accelerate [22] for efficient scaling across mul-
tiple GPUs and compute nodes. This implementation pre-
serves the simplicity of single-GPU training while enabling
near-linear scaling to large clusters for high-throughput vi-
sual sim-to-real learning. We identify scaling up GPUs for
both teacher and student training as critical in our ablation                        Figure 7. Real-world performance comparison: VIRAL
studies in Figure 14 and Figure 15.                                                  matches expert-level reliability, outperforms non-experts, and op-
                                                                                     erates faster than the expert teleoperator.

erage, which in turn improves robustness. Overall, these                  compact, RGB-driven visuomotor policies trained in ran-
results indicate that substantial computing is not merely a               domized simulation to support real-time, goal-conditioned
convenience but a practical requirement for reliable visual               locomotion without sacrificing sim-to-real scalability.
loco-manipulation distillation.
                                                                          Sim-to-Real for Manipulation Visual sim-to-real has
                                                                          been a key driver of progress in manipulation. A central
                                                                          tool is domain randomization: by varying rendering prop-
                                                                          erties in simulation, policies trained on RGB can transfer
                                                                          to the real world [53, 58, 66]. This strategy enabled end-
                                                                          to-end RL for challenging skills—e.g., OpenAI’s Dactyl re-
                                                                          oriented objects with a five-finger hand using massive ran-

lation loss (left) and success rate (right) when training with 1–64       scaled to tasks like Rubik’s Cube solving and high-speed
GPUs. Larger GPU counts provide significantly faster conver-
                                                                          rotation [2, 24]. Early attempts that relied on high-fidelity
gence, smoother optimization dynamics, and higher final perfor-
                                                                          RGB/depth/point-cloud simulation still struggled with the
mance, highlighting the importance of large-scale parallel simula-
tion for vision-based loco-manipulation.                                  reality gap [2, 3, 25, 30, 33, 75, 76]. Recent methods
                                                                          improve robustness and scalability via a teacher–student
4.9. Object generalization                                                paradigm: a privileged-state teacher is trained first, then a
                                                                          student is distilled from RGB with randomization [17, 42,
We study object-level generalization on the grasping sub-

task under two training regimes: (i) single-object training

                                                                          control, using either modular architectures that decouple leg
                                                                          and arm [6, 14, 42] or end-to-end policies that coordinate

Sim-to-Real for Locomotion Sim-to-real techniques                         6. Limitations and Discussions
have enabled blind locomotion policies trained in simu-
lation to be deployed zero-shot on real legged robots [6,                 While sim-to-real has demonstrated remarkable success in
11, 18, 20, 31, 35–38, 40, 63]. These proprioceptive poli-                isolated capabilities—robust locomotion, geometric per-

quired to ground these features in reality. We can, with

ronment for a single task (e.g., dishwashing) requires mod-            field has successfully identified the sweet spot for sim-to-

fordances, varied states (dirty vs. clean), and interaction            ited parameters (terrain, mass) and carefully-designed re-

during real-world deployment (e.g., adapting to a pet’s in-                We believe the path forward involves redefining the role

constraints). Current asset taxonomies and generative pro-             than forcing simulation to generate the entire distribution

                                                                   (1) walking toward the object; (2) moving the arm and hand
